title: Don't Make Me Think — UI/UX guidelines
premise: Steve Krug's rule: a page should be self-evident. Every question a person has to stop and answer — what is this, where do I click, did that work — is a small tax on their attention. These guidelines exist to remove those questions, not to decorate the removal.

topics.motion: Motion design, microinteractions, Lottie and Rive

principles.title: Visibility of system status
principles.principle: The interface always tells people what is happening, through feedback that arrives fast enough to feel like a reply.
principles.why: Silence reads as breakage. A person who does not know whether their click registered will click again, or leave.
rules: Acknowledge every action within 100ms, even if the result takes longer — a pressed state counts.
Show progress for anything past ~1s; show remaining time or a determinate bar past ~10s.
Never leave a submitted form in the same visual state it had before submission.

principles.title: Match between the system and the real world
principles.principle: Speak the user's language — their words, their concepts, their ordering — not the system's internals.
principles.why: Interface vocabulary is the signposting people navigate by. Naming things after your implementation forces them to learn your architecture before they can use your product.
rules: Name controls after what the person does, never after how it is built.
Order information the way the task runs, not the way the data model is shaped.
Use the units, date formats and conventions of the reader's locale.

principles.title: User control and freedom
principles.principle: People pick the wrong thing constantly. Every path in needs a visible path out.
principles.why: Fear of being trapped makes people explore less, which makes them slower at everything else.
rules: Offer undo rather than a confirmation dialog wherever the action is reversible.
Make cancel always available and never the destructive default.
Never trap keyboard focus in a component the user cannot escape with Escape.

principles.title: Consistency and standards
principles.principle: The same thing looks the same and is called the same everywhere. Platform conventions win over invention.
principles.why: People spend most of their time on other sites. What they have already learned there is the cheapest thing you can give them.
rules: One action keeps one name through the whole flow: a button that says Publish produces a toast that says Published.
Do not restyle a native control into something that behaves differently from what it looks like.
Links look like links, buttons look like buttons, and each does what its appearance promises.

principles.title: Error prevention
principles.principle: Designing the mistake out beats explaining it afterwards.
principles.why: The best error message is the one that never had to be written.
rules: Constrain input to what is valid instead of validating free text after the fact.
Separate destructive controls from routine ones by distance, not just colour.
Warn before the point of no return, and only there — a confirmation on everything trains people to dismiss confirmations.

principles.title: Recognition rather than recall
principles.principle: Show the options. Do not make people remember something from one screen to use it on the next.
principles.why: Recognition is nearly free; recall is expensive and fails under stress.
rules: Keep the information needed for a step visible during that step.
Label icons unless the icon is universally understood — and almost none are.
Carry entered values forward instead of asking twice (WCAG 3.3.7).

principles.title: Flexibility and efficiency of use
principles.principle: Serve the first-time user and the thousandth-time user without making either pay for the other.
principles.why: Accelerators are invisible to novices and decisive for experts.
rules: Add keyboard shortcuts for the actions people repeat, and surface them in tooltips.
Let frequent paths be personalised or remembered rather than re-navigated.
Never gate a fast path behind an onboarding the expert has to sit through again.

principles.title: Aesthetic and minimalist design
principles.principle: Every element competes with every other for attention. Anything that is not needed weakens what is.
principles.why: Minimalism here is not a style — it is a ratio. Cutting the unnecessary raises the visibility of the necessary.
rules: Cut anything that does not help the page's single job.
Prefer progressive disclosure to a screen that shows everything at once.
Give the primary action one visual treatment nothing else on the page shares.

principles.title: Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
principles.principle: An error says what happened, in plain words, and what to do next.
principles.why: An error that only announces failure leaves the person exactly where they were stuck.
rules: No codes without prose, and no prose without a next step.
Put the message next to the thing that went wrong, not only in a banner.
Do not apologise or blame — state the problem and the fix.

principles.title: Help and documentation
principles.principle: Ideally none is needed; realistically it must be findable, searchable and task-shaped.
principles.why: People reach documentation mid-task, already frustrated, and will not read a manual to finish one step.
rules: Put help where the task is, not only in a separate section.
Keep help in the same relative place on every page (WCAG 3.2.6).
Write it as steps to a goal, not as a description of features.

principles.title: Hick's Law — decision time grows with choices
principles.principle: The time to decide increases with the number and complexity of the options presented.
principles.why: Every extra option is work the person did not ask for. Choice overload reads as complexity even when each choice is simple.
rules: Keep top-level navigation to roughly 5–7 items; beyond that, group.
Highlight one recommended option instead of presenting equals.
Break long forms and flows into steps rather than one dense screen.
Do not simplify to the point of abstraction — a vague label is a slower decision than a longer clear one.

principles.title: Fitts's Law — target size and distance
principles.principle: The time to hit a target is a function of its size and how far away it is. Small and far is slow and error-prone.
principles.why: Speed and accuracy trade against each other. Small targets do not just take longer, they produce wrong clicks.
rules: Make interactive targets at least 24×24 CSS px, and 44×44 for anything primary or touch-first.
Leave spacing between adjacent targets so a near miss does nothing rather than the wrong thing.
Put the action near the content it acts on — travel distance is part of the cost.
Screen edges and corners are effectively infinite targets; use them for high-frequency controls.

principles.title: Doherty Threshold — stay under 400ms
principles.principle: Interaction below roughly 400ms keeps a person in flow; above it, they start waiting on the machine.
principles.why: Attention leaks at the pause. Perceived speed is a usability property, not a performance metric.
rules: Respond to input in under 100ms, complete common actions in under 400ms.
Use optimistic UI where the action is nearly certain to succeed and cheap to reverse.
If you cannot be fast, be informative — a determinate progress indicator changes the felt duration.

principles.title: Text alternatives (1.1.1, A)
principles.principle: Every non-text element that carries meaning has a text equivalent; every decorative one is hidden from assistive technology.
principles.why: An unlabelled image is a dead end for a screen reader user, and a decorative image announced aloud is noise.
rules: Meaningful images get alt text describing their purpose, not their appearance.
Decorative images get alt="" and inline SVGs get aria-hidden="true".
Icon-only buttons carry an accessible name via aria-label or visually hidden text.

principles.title: Contrast (1.4.3 AA, 1.4.11 AA)
principles.principle: Body text needs 4.5:1 against its background, large text 3:1, and UI components and graphical objects 3:1.
principles.why: Contrast is the single most common accessibility failure on the web, and it degrades for everyone in sunlight or on a cheap panel.
rules: 4.5:1 for text under 24px (or under 19px bold); 3:1 above that.
3:1 for borders, icons and focus indicators that convey meaning.
Never rely on colour alone to convey state — pair it with text, shape or an icon (1.4.1).

principles.title: Resize and reflow (1.4.4 AA, 1.4.10 AA)
principles.principle: Text scales to 200% and content reflows to a 320px-wide viewport without loss of information or two-dimensional scrolling.
principles.why: Zoom is the most used accessibility feature there is. Blocking it breaks the page for people who never identify as disabled.
rules: Never set user-scalable=no or maximum-scale on the viewport meta tag.
Size text in rem or em so it responds to the user's font-size preference.
Test at 320px width and at 200% zoom; nothing should require horizontal scrolling except data tables and code.

principles.title: Focus visible and not obscured (2.4.7 AA, 2.4.11 AA, 2.4.13 AAA)
principles.principle: Keyboard focus is always visible, at least partially unobscured, and clearly distinguishable from the unfocused state.
principles.why: For a keyboard or switch user, the focus ring is the cursor. Removing it is removing the pointer.
rules: Never write outline: none without providing a replacement indicator on :focus-visible.
Focus indicators need at least a 2px perimeter and 3:1 contrast against the unfocused state (2.4.13).
Sticky headers and footers must not hide the focused element (2.4.11).

principles.title: Target size minimum (2.5.8, AA)
principles.principle: Pointer targets are at least 24×24 CSS px, or spaced so that 24px circles centred on them do not overlap.
principles.why: Hand tremor, a moving bus, or a thumb on a large phone all make small adjacent targets a coin flip.
rules: 24×24 is the floor, not the goal — 44×44 for primary and touch-first controls.
Inline links within a sentence are exempt; standalone controls are not.
Padding counts toward target size, so grow the hit area rather than the glyph.

principles.title: Dragging movements (2.5.7, AA)
principles.principle: Anything operable by dragging has a single-pointer alternative, unless dragging is essential.
principles.why: Holding and moving accurately is exactly what a tremor, a trackpad, or a switch device makes hard.
rules: Reorderable lists need up/down controls alongside drag handles.
Sliders need keyboard arrow support and, ideally, a numeric input.
Map and canvas panning needs buttons or keyboard equivalents.

principles.title: Accessible authentication (3.3.8, AA)
principles.principle: Do not require solving, recalling or transcribing anything to log in.
principles.why: A cognitive function test at the door excludes people before they reach the product.
rules: Allow paste and password managers on every credential field.
Offer an alternative to puzzle or memory-based authentication — a link sent by email qualifies.
Do not ask for the same information twice in one process (3.3.7).

principles.title: Structure, semantics and landmarks (1.3.1 A, 2.4.6 AA)
principles.principle: The document's structure is expressed in markup, not only in appearance: one h1, a nested heading order, real landmarks, real controls.
principles.why: Assistive technology navigates by structure. A page that only looks structured is unnavigable.
rules: One h1 per page and no skipped heading levels.
Use header, nav, main, footer instead of divs with classes.
Use button for actions and a for navigation; a div with a click handler is neither focusable nor announced.
Set lang on the html element.

principles.title: Plain, literal language
principles.principle: Write short, concrete, literal sentences. Idioms, metaphor and irony are barriers, not personality.
principles.why: Autistic readers frequently process language literally; readers with ADHD or dyslexia lose the thread in long sentences. Neither is helped by cleverness.
rules: One idea per sentence, active voice, no figures of speech.
Expand acronyms on first use, on every page.
Never label a button 'Click here' or 'Learn more' — say what happens.
Front-load the point; do not build to it.

principles.title: Visual calm over visual intensity
principles.principle: Avoid bright clashing colours, dense walls of text and cluttered layouts. Give content room.
principles.why: Sensory overload is a real exit condition. What reads as 'vibrant' to one person is unusable to another.
rules: Avoid saturated complementary colours next to each other at large areas.
Break text into short paragraphs with headings and generous line height (1.5+).
Keep line length around 60–75 characters.
Use whitespace as structure rather than borders and boxes everywhere.

principles.title: Predictability and user control over change
principles.principle: Nothing moves, appears, or changes context without the person causing it.
principles.why: Unexpected change costs re-orientation, which is expensive for ADHD and autistic users in particular, and disorienting for everyone.
rules: No auto-playing carousels, videos or audio.
No content that shifts after load — reserve space for anything that arrives late.
Do not change context on focus or on input (WCAG 3.2.1, 3.2.2).
Let people pause, stop or hide anything that moves for more than 5 seconds (WCAG 2.2.2).

principles.title: No arbitrary time pressure
principles.principle: Do not impose deadlines the task does not require, and never lose someone's work to a timeout.
principles.why: Time limits convert a manageable task into a stressful one, and stress narrows working memory further.
rules: Warn before a session expires and allow extension (WCAG 2.2.1).
Preserve entered data across a timeout or a back navigation.
Avoid countdowns and scarcity timers; they are a dark pattern that hits anxious users hardest.

principles.title: These are heuristics, and users disagree
principles.principle: Neurodivergence is not one profile. Guidance that helps one reader can hinder another, so preferences beat defaults.
principles.why: The GOV.UK dyslexia poster recommends left-aligned text; a dyslexic commenter on that very post said justified text is what keeps them from losing the line. Both are true of different people.
rules: Where guidance conflicts, offer the choice rather than picking for everyone.
Respect OS-level preferences before your own defaults: reduced motion, contrast, colour scheme, font size.
Test with real users; a checklist is a starting point, not evidence.

principles.title: Motion has a job or it does not ship
principles.principle: Animation exists to explain a change: where a thing came from, where it went, what is now different. Decorative motion is cost without payment.
principles.why: Motion is the most attention-grabbing thing on a screen. Spending that on decoration means having nothing left for the moments that matter.
rules: Animate to show causality, continuity or hierarchy — never to fill silence.
Spend the boldest motion on one signature moment; keep everything around it quiet.
If removing an animation costs the user nothing, remove it.

principles.title: Timing and easing
principles.principle: UI motion lives between roughly 150ms and 400ms, with easing that matches the direction of travel.
principles.why: Under 100ms reads as an instant cut; over 500ms the person is waiting on an animation, which is worse than no animation.
rules: 150–250ms for small changes (hover, toggle), 250–400ms for larger transitions.
ease-out for things entering, ease-in for things leaving, ease-in-out for things moving in place.
Never animate a blocking transition longer than 400ms.
Animate transform and opacity; animating layout properties drops frames.

principles.title: Respect prefers-reduced-motion
principles.principle: Every motion design has a reduced variant, and the reduced variant is not 'broken with the animation removed'.
principles.why: Vestibular disorders make large motion physically sickening. The OS setting is a medical preference, not a style choice.
rules: Wrap non-essential motion in a prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference guard, or neutralise it under reduce.
Under reduce, keep state changes legible — cross-fade instead of translating, or cut instantly.
Parallax, auto-scroll and large-scale zooms are the highest-risk patterns; drop them entirely under reduce.
Pause Lottie and Rive playback under reduce rather than merely hiding the canvas.

principles.title: Microinteractions and instant feedback
principles.principle: Every interactive element acknowledges input immediately, in the same place the input happened.
principles.why: The gap between action and acknowledgement is where doubt lives. Closing it under 100ms removes the doubt entirely.
rules: Give every control hover, active, focus-visible and disabled states — all four.
Acknowledge press within 100ms even when the result takes seconds.
Put the feedback at the point of interaction, not only in a corner toast.
Make success and failure feel different in more than colour: shape, position or motion too.
Never animate away a message the person has not had time to read.

principles.title: Choosing Lottie or Rive — and whether to use either
principles.principle: CSS and the Web Animations API cost nothing at runtime. Reach for a vector animation runtime only when the animation is beyond their reach.
principles.why: Rive's WASM renderer adds roughly 200KB and dotLottie roughly 50KB before a single frame plays. That is a real budget being spent on something CSS may already do.
rules: Default to CSS transitions and keyframes; they are composited, cost zero bytes, and respect reduced motion trivially.
Use Lottie (prefer .lottie over raw .json — around 80% smaller) for designer-authored, timeline-based illustrations that play through.
Use Rive when the animation must respond to state: its state machine is the reason to pay the bundle cost, not its file size.
File size is no longer a meaningful differentiator between .lottie and .riv; choose on interactivity and tooling.
Lazy-load the runtime and the asset, and never block first paint on either.
Give every animation a text equivalent or aria-hidden — a canvas is invisible to assistive technology.

principles.title: SVG craft — detail that survives scaling
principles.principle: A beautiful SVG is built on a consistent grid with intentional geometry, not traced from a raster and cleaned up afterwards.
principles.why: Vector art is read at every size. Inconsistent stroke weights and off-grid coordinates read as sloppiness precisely because the format cannot hide them.
rules: Draw on a consistent viewBox (24, 48 or 64 units) and keep coordinates on the grid.
Keep stroke widths consistent across a set, and use vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke where scale must not thicken lines.
Prefer stroke-linecap: round and stroke-linejoin: round for warmth, square for precision — pick one per set and hold it.
Build depth with layered fills, gradients and opacity rather than raster shadows.
Use currentColor for anything that should inherit text colour, so one icon serves every theme.
Optimise the path data — remove editor metadata, round coordinates to 2 decimals, merge duplicate paths.
Give meaningful SVGs a <title> and role="img"; give decorative ones aria-hidden="true".

principles.title: SVG animation — technique by intent
principles.principle: Animate SVG with the cheapest technique that achieves the intent, and let the drawing itself carry the detail.
principles.why: SVG can be animated four different ways with wildly different costs. Choosing by habit rather than by intent is where performance and accessibility problems come from.
rules: Line drawing: animate stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset — one property, composited, no dependency.
Morphing between shapes: requires matching point counts; author both states from the same base path.
Transforms on SVG children: prefer CSS transform with transform-box: fill-box and an explicit transform-origin, or coordinates go somewhere surprising.
Stagger related elements by 30–60ms rather than firing them together; sequence is what makes motion feel authored.
Do not animate filter or complex masks per frame — they are not composited and will drop frames.
Keep SMIL out of new work; CSS and the Web Animations API are better supported and controllable.
Everything here is still motion: guard it with prefers-reduced-motion.

principles.title: Light theme is the default
principles.principle: Ship a light theme. Offer a dark alternative only where the niche genuinely demands it, and never as the only option.
principles.why: Light-on-dark reduces reading accuracy for most sighted readers and is actively worse for people with astigmatism, where light text on dark backgrounds smears. Dark mode is a preference for a minority of contexts, not a neutral default.
rules: The default palette — with no media query and no toggle — must be the light one.
Do not set color-scheme: dark alone, and do not define a dark palette without a light one.
Justify a dark option by the niche: prolonged low-light use, media viewing, code editing, astronomy, camera and photo tools. 'It looks modern' is not a justification.
When a dark theme exists, drive it from prefers-color-scheme and let an explicit toggle override the system, never the reverse.
A dark theme is not an inverted light theme: reduce contrast slightly, desaturate, and re-check every contrast ratio.

principles.title: Lightness is a feature
principles.principle: Weight is felt as sluggishness, and sluggishness is felt as bad design. The fastest asset is the one not sent.
principles.why: Perceived performance is inseparable from perceived quality. A beautiful page that takes three seconds is not a beautiful page.
rules: Budget the critical path: HTML plus critical CSS under 100KB compressed.
Self-host fonts, subset them, and limit to two families and the weights actually used.
Use font-display: swap or optional so text never waits on a font.
Give every image explicit width and height, or aspect-ratio, to reserve space and prevent layout shift.
Lazy-load anything below the fold, and never lazy-load the LCP element.
Defer non-critical JavaScript; nothing above the fold should wait on a script.
Use content-visibility: auto on long off-screen sections, with contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar stays stable.

principles.title: Responsive by intrinsic sizing, not by breakpoint list
principles.principle: Let content decide when the layout changes. Breakpoints tied to device widths are a maintenance treadmill.
principles.why: There is no canonical set of device sizes, and there never was. Layouts that respond to their own content survive hardware you have not seen.
rules: Prefer clamp(), min(), max() and fluid type scales to fixed steps.
Use container queries for components so a card lays itself out by its own width, not the viewport's.
Design mobile-first: the small layout is the constrained one and should be authored first.
Never let the page scroll horizontally; wide content (tables, code, diagrams) scrolls inside its own container.
Test at 320px, at 200% zoom, and in landscape on a short viewport.

principles.title: Do not assume the input device
principles.principle: Screen size does not tell you whether there is a mouse, a finger, a stylus or a keyboard. Assume all of them.
principles.why: Touch laptops, desktop touchscreens and tablets with trackpads all break the width-implies-input assumption.
rules: Never gate functionality behind hover — hover is an enhancement, not an affordance.
Use pointer: coarse and any-hover for capability, never viewport width.
Every pointer interaction has a keyboard equivalent.
Size for touch everywhere; a large target harms nobody with a mouse.
